summary: DP950-1 is the austenite–ferrite duplex, ultralow-density Fe-Mn-Al-C-Cr lightweight steel specimen obtained by annealing a cold-rolled 30Mn-13Al-1.3C-5Cr sheet at 950 °C for 1 min followed by water quenching — the short-time, low-temperature end of the paper's 600–1050 °C, 1–5 min annealing series. It exhibits a partially recrystallized austenite matrix containing both granular α ferrite and banded δ ferrite in an unusually large total ferrite amount, which gives it the highest tensile strength but the lowest ductility of the annealed specimens (UTS 1440 MPa, SUTS 226.4 MPa·g⁻¹·cm³, TE 5.2%), making it the contrast case that motivates the study's duplex-microstructure design for strength–ductility–density synergy.
composition: Nominal composition of the designed lightweight steel: Fe–30.35Mn–12.60Al–1.32C–4.83Cr (wt%, weight percentage), with a measured ultralow density of 6.36 g·cm⁻³ (by buoyancy balance according to Archimedes' Principle). The alloy is a redesign of the earlier ultralow-density austenitic steel 29.05Mn–12.01Al–1.48C–5.13Cr (6.34 g·cm⁻³, the prior record), reformulated to produce an austenite–ferrite duplex microstructure. About 5 wt% Cr is added specifically to suppress the formation of brittle intergranular κ-carbides; Mn, Al and C are the principal lightening and strengthening elements, with high Mn/Al/C contents in austenite enabling extensive precipitation of κ-carbide nanoparticles. The ferrite-forming chemistry is exploited because the BCC structure has a lower atomic density than FCC, making ferrite more effective than austenite at reducing density.
processing: Processing sequence: (1) vacuum induction melting under an argon atmosphere and casting into an ingot; (2) forging the ingot to a thick slab; (3) homogenization at 1200 °C for 2 h prior to hot rolling; (4) hot rolling (HR) to 6 mm thickness; (5) solution treatment — the HR plate heated to 1050 °C, isothermally held for 0.5 h, then water quenched; (6) cold rolling (CR) to 3 mm thickness, the parent CR state shared by all DP specimens; (7) annealing at 950 °C for 1 min, which defines the state label DP950-1 (XXX = annealing temperature, Y = annealing period); (8) water quenching again. DP950-1 thus corresponds to the lowest temperature and shortest time (950 °C, 1 min) of the paper's 600–1050 °C, 1–5 min annealing matrix applied to the common cold-rolled precursor.
microstructure: Austenite (FCC) matrix in a partially recrystallized condition — recrystallized γ fraction 19.4% (GROD <2°) — with an average γ grain size of 14.64 ± 8.88 µm; the GROD map shows mixed yellow (recrystallized) and red/pink (deformed) regions together with a heavy black high-angle boundary network, and shear bands inherited from cold rolling are retained. Two morphologically distinct ferrites coexist in the BCC phase: granular α ferrite (19.6% by EBSD) located at austenite grain boundaries and triple points, and banded δ ferrite (9.8% by EBSD) elongated along the rolling direction and traceable to the preceding hot-rolled/solidified structure. The total ferrite content is therefore high (~29.4%). Annealing at 950 °C produces the coarsest δ and α ferrite grains as well as the largest ferrite amount among the studied conditions, and brittle intergranular κ-carbides (2–3 µm) and Cr₇C₃ carbides form during this anneal (κ-carbides at grain boundaries and BCC/FCC interfaces; Cr₇C₃ both several-micron coarse particles inside ferrite bands and hundreds-of-nanometre particles at grain boundaries). The ferrite fraction by XRD for DP950-1 is not reported. By nanoindentation (measured on DP1000-5), ferrite is clearly softer than the recrystallized austenite.
properties: Room-temperature uniaxial tensile properties measured along the rolling direction (flat dog-bone specimens, 25 mm gage length, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹, average of three measurements): yield strength 1015 ± 5 MPa, ultimate tensile strength 1440 ± 10 MPa, total elongation 5.2 ± 0.2%. Specific yield strength 159.6 ± 0.8 MPa·g⁻¹·cm³ and specific ultimate tensile strength 226.4 ± 1.6 MPa·g⁻¹·cm³ (density 6.36 g·cm⁻³). DP950-1 has the highest UTS and SUTS but the lowest total elongation of all annealed specimens; increasing the annealing time to 5 min (DP950-5) lowers both YS and UTS by about 90 MPa without improving ductility. Characterization techniques applied across the alloy/specimen series: X-ray diffraction (2θ 35–80°), scanning electron microscopy (ZEISS Gemini 300), transmission electron microscopy (FEI Tecnai G20) with SAED and EDS, electron backscatter diffraction (Scanning Auger Nanoprobe, PHI 710), and nanoindentation.
mechanisms: Annealing of the cold-rolled structure at 950 °C for 1 min (the lowest temperature/shortest time of the series) produces the coarsest δ and α ferrite grains together with the largest total ferrite amount (α 19.6% + δ 9.8% by EBSD, ≈29.4%), because austenite-to-ferrite transformation occurs on heating to 950 °C while ferrite-to-austenite transformation only becomes dominant above this temperature.

The large ferrite content of DP950-1 causes incompatible straining at the numerous interfaces between the soft ferrite and the much harder unrecrystallized (unRexed) austenite, owing to the great difference in their strength/hardness, so cracks initiate and propagate easily at/along the ferrite–austenite interfaces, which explains the poor ductility (TE 5.2%) of DP950-1.

Only 19.4% of the austenite is recrystallized at 950 °C/1 min, so the matrix remains largely in the deformed (unRexed) state with retained cold-rolling shear bands; this partial-recrystallization condition is the microstructural reason the specimen is strong but brittle.

Granular α ferrite grains located at austenite boundaries and triple points can restrain austenite grain growth, but at 950 °C this restraining effect is limited by the concurrent coarsening of both α and δ ferrite, giving DP950-1 the largest austenite grain size (14.64 ± 8.88 µm) among the annealed states.

During annealing at 950 °C the reaction austenite → ferrite + Cr₇C₃ carbides + intergranular κ-carbides takes place; the coarse intergranular κ-carbides are inherently brittle and further degrade ductility, whereas raising the temperature to 1000–1050 °C dissolves these carbides and promotes ferrite-to-austenite transformation and full recrystallization, which is why DP1000-5/DP1050-1 recover both YS and TE.

Because the granular α ferrite grains are softer than the recrystallized austenite, specimens annealed at 950 °C (ferrite-rich) show lower YS than specimens annealed at higher temperatures where harder austenite dominates the matrix.
conclusions: DP950-1 represents the ferrite-rich, partially recrystallized end of the annealing series: at 950 °C for 1 min the ferrite amount reaches its maximum and the austenite is only 19.4% recrystallized, giving the highest UTS (1440 MPa) and highest SUTS (226.4 MPa·g⁻¹·cm³) but the lowest total elongation (5.2%) of the annealed specimens. It serves as the contrast to the optimized DP1000-5 (1000 °C/5 min: UTS 1250 MPa, TE 41.4%, SUTS×TE >8 GPa·g⁻¹·cm³·%), demonstrating that excessive ferrite and incomplete recrystallization must be avoided. The overall study shows that an austenite–ferrite duplex microstructural design in an ultralow-density Fe-Mn-Al-C-Cr steel is a promising route to strength–ductility–density synergy — granular α ferrite restraining austenite grain growth, δ ferrite bands capturing/deflecting/blunting cracks, and high Mn/Al/C austenite providing nanosized κ-carbide precipitation strengthening — provided the ferrite content and morphology are optimized by annealing.

In the SUTS-versus-TE comparison plot (Fig. 3b), DP950-1 lies among 'Our steel' data points but its SUTS×TE product falls well below the 8 GPa·g⁻¹·cm³·% contour because of its very low elongation, unlike DP1000-5 and DP1050-1 which exceed the 8 contour.
